readerTitle: He had the numbers. He still lost the account.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (식품 유통 영업 담당자와 동네 마트, 레스토랑 단체 예약) + 실제 개념·연구 (Chris Voss의 '전술적 공감', 감정 이름 붙이기 연구)
insight: 상대의 감정과 입장을 소리 내어 짚어 주는 것은 양보가 아니라, 상대가 진짜 원하는 것을 꺼내 놓게 만드는 정보 수집 도구다.
misconception: 공감은 상대에게 져 주거나 사과하며 깎아 주는 것이고, 협상은 더 정확한 사실과 근거를 내미는 쪽이 이긴다.

sources.text: Voss, C. & Raz, T. (2016). Never Split the Difference: Negotiating As If Your Life Depended On It. Harper Business.
Lieberman, M. D. et al. (2007). Putting Feelings Into Words: Affect Labeling Disrupts Amygdala Activity in Response to Affective Stimuli. Psychological Science, 18(5), 421–428.
마트·레스토랑 사례와 수치(정시 배송률 98%, 15% 할인, 12% 인상)는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 'tactical empathy'라는 용어를 Chris Voss가 2016년 책에서 대중화했다는 표현을 확인하세요. 용어를 처음 만든 사람이라고 쓰지 않고 'popularized'로만 적었습니다.
Lieberman et al.(2007)은 감정에 이름을 붙이면 편도체 반응이 줄어든다는 fMRI 연구입니다. 실험실 연구라서 협상 효과를 직접 증명하지는 않습니다. 카드에는 'suggests'로 약하게 표현했습니다.
마트와 레스토랑 사례는 모두 가상입니다. 98%, 15%, 12%, 6년 같은 수치에는 실제 근거가 없고 계산도 들어 있지 않습니다.
SAL-05-09(인질 협상가)와 겹치지 않도록 FBI 배경은 한 문장으로만 언급했습니다.

cards.title: He had the numbers. He still lost the account.
body: A sales rep for a food distributor visits one of his biggest customers, a family grocery store. The owner is furious. A delivery arrived late before a holiday weekend.
The rep comes prepared with a printout showing a 98% on-time rate this year. He walks the owner through it line by line.
A month later, the store signs with a rival distributor.

image.label: A sales rep holding a chart while a store owner stands by empty shelves
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 텅 빈 마트 진열대 앞에서 팔짱 낀 가게 주인과 '98%' 그래프 종이를 내미는 영업 담당자. 두 사람 사이에 보이지 않는 벽이 있는 느낌. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The owner is shouting. What do you say first?
body: You're the rep. The owner says: "Your truck showed up at noon on Friday. My shelves were empty all morning. I'm done with you."

options.text: "Let me show you our numbers. We're on time 98% of the time."
options.feedback: The facts are true, but they answer a question he didn't ask. To him, it sounds like his bad Friday doesn't count.

options.text: "I'm so sorry. We'll take 15% off your next order."
options.feedback: It calms the moment, but you pay before learning what he actually needs. It also teaches him that anger earns discounts.

options.text: "It sounds like that morning cost you sales and made you look bad to your regulars."
options.feedback: You haven't agreed to anything or given anything away. You've shown you understand, which makes it easier for him to tell you what he wants.

cards.title: Right facts, wrong conversation.
body: The rep's data wasn't wrong. It was beside the point. The owner wasn't arguing about averages. He was upset about one Friday, his empty shelves and the customers who walked out.
People who feel unheard either repeat themselves louder or leave. Every fact the rep added made the owner feel more dismissed.
The real issue came out later, and it was simple: he needed holiday deliveries before 7 a.m.

cards.title: Tactical empathy
body: **Tactical empathy** means working out how the other side sees the situation and how they feel about it, then saying it out loud so they know you get it.

Former FBI negotiator Chris Voss popularized the term in his 2016 book *Never Split the Difference*. The word *tactical* matters. You're not agreeing, and you're not giving in. You're making it safe for them to tell you what really matters.

image.label: Two people at a table, one naming the other's feeling in a speech bubble
image.brief: 협상 테이블 양쪽에 두 사람. 한 사람의 말풍선에 "It sounds like...", 맞은편 사람 머리 위의 먹구름이 조금 걷히고 작은 열쇠가 나타남. 단순하고 따뜻한 인포그래픽 톤.

cards.softwareNote: An angry support ticket from a big account works the same way. "It sounds like this outage hit you during your busiest week" usually gets further than a link to the uptime dashboard. Once the customer feels heard, they'll often tell you what would keep them from churning.

cards.title: Name it, then go quiet.
body: The basic tool is a **label**: a short guess, said out loud, at what the other person feels or worries about.
list: Start with "It sounds like…" or "It seems like…" instead of "I understand"
Name their feeling or what's at stake for them, not your defense
Stop talking. Let them confirm or correct you
Only then move on to facts and options
cards.callout: Brain-imaging research suggests that putting feelings into words can dampen strong emotional reactions. A calmer person can think about a deal.

cards.title: Empathy is not a discount.
body: Picture a second rep with the same complaint. He says: "I totally understand, I'm so sorry, here's 15% off." The owner takes it. Next month he complains again, louder.

That rep offered sympathy plus a **concession**, and he used money to soothe feelings. Tactical empathy soothes feelings with understanding. It saves concessions for later, when you know what they should buy you.

cards.title: Fake empathy is worse than none.
body: People spot scripts. A flat "I hear your frustration" followed by "but" tells them you were just waiting for your turn to talk. A wrong label is fine if you let them correct it. A canned one isn't.
Empathy also doesn't replace fixing the problem. If the trucks stay late, no sentence will save the account. And if people notice you're naming feelings only to manipulate them, you lose their trust.

cards.title: Now it's a restaurant.
body: A company has held its year-end dinner at your restaurant for six years. Food costs rose, so this year's quote is 12% higher.
The organizer calls: "After six years, this is how you treat us?" What do you do first?

options.text: Email her the supplier invoices that explain the increase
options.feedback: It's a fair case, but it argues about price while she's talking about loyalty. She'll probably go and get three other quotes.

options.text: Say, "It sounds like you feel your loyalty isn't being noticed," then listen
options.feedback: You deal with her real complaint first. She may tell you what would feel fair, such as a price locked for two years or a welcome drink, and that could cost you less than 12%.

options.text: Cancel the increase to keep her happy
options.feedback: You keep the booking but absorb the cost. You also never find out whether price was the real issue.

cards.title: Name what they feel before you argue what's true.
body: Facts win arguments. Deals get made when people feel understood.
**Try it today:** in your next tense conversation, say one "It sounds like…" sentence before you explain anything. Then wait for the answer.
